key_terms.meaning: P: the original readable message that is encrypted.
C: the scrambled output produced by encryption.
K: the secret parameter that controls encryption and decryption.
Each plaintext symbol is replaced by another symbol using a keyed mapping.
Symbols keep their identities but their positions are rearranged.
Pr[C = c | P = p0] = Pr[C = c | P = p1] for every plaintext pair and every ciphertext c.
C = P ⊕ K, where K is random, as long as P, and used only once.
A deterministic algorithm that stretches a short random seed into a long output indistinguishable from random.
S: the pseudorandom bit string that a stream cipher XORs with the plaintext.
Encrypts one symbol or bit at a time as C_i = P_i ⊕ S_i.
A keyed permutation E_K on fixed-size n-bit blocks.
A round splits the block into L and R, computes L′ = R and R′ = L ⊕ F(R, K_i), then swaps; decryption uses reversed subkeys.
16 Feistel rounds on 64-bit blocks with a 56-bit effective key and eight S-boxes.
EDE construction C = E_K3(D_K2(E_K1(P))), used with two-key or three-key variants.
A byte-oriented substitution-permutation network with 10, 12 or 14 rounds for 128, 192 or 256-bit keys.
A rule that uses a block cipher to encrypt arbitrary-length messages with an IV, nonce or counter.
Finds linear equations in plaintext, ciphertext and key bits that hold with bias away from 1/2.
Tracks input difference ΔP to output difference ΔC through rounds with high probability.
The adversary may request encryptions of chosen plaintexts and still cannot distinguish challenge ciphertexts.
The adversary may also request decryptions of chosen ciphertexts, except the challenge ciphertext, and cannot distinguish.

takeaways: Classical ciphers hide letters by substitution or transposition, but frequency and pattern analysis often breaks them.
Perfect secrecy is possible only when the key is at least as long as the message and is never reused, as in the one-time pad.
A pseudorandom generator turns a short secret seed into a long keystream, so a stream cipher can encrypt bit by bit.
A Feistel round need not be invertible because the swap and XOR structure gives decryption when subkeys are reversed.
DES is a 16-round Feistel cipher with a short 56-bit key, so triple DES extends its useful life by repeated encryption.
AES replaces DES as a faster byte-oriented SPN with longer keys and no Feistel half-swap.
Modes of operation adapt a block cipher to real messages, but ECB leaks patterns and CBC or CTR needs a unique IV or nonce.
Linear and differential cryptanalysis show why round count, S-box choice and key size matter, and modern security is stated with CPA and CCA attack games.
bank_note: Long answers usually stress comparing Feistel and SPN designs, tracing DES and AES rounds and key schedules, choosing modes for given applications, and defining CPA and CCA security with cryptanalysis limits.

bank.q: Explain substitution and transposition ciphers with one example each. Why do letter-frequency and pattern analysis make classical ciphers weak?
outline: Define plaintext, ciphertext and key.
Give a substitution example such as Caesar or a monoalphabetic mapping.
Give a transposition example such as columnar rearrangement.
Explain frequency analysis on substituted letters and pattern leakage in rearranged text.
State why a large key space alone does not prevent statistical attacks.

bank.q: Define perfect secrecy. Show how the one-time pad reaches it and explain its practical limitations.
outline: State Pr[C = c | P = p0] = Pr[C = c | P = p1] for all plaintexts and ciphertexts.
Define one-time pad encryption C = P ⊕ K and decryption P = C ⊕ K.
Argue that a uniform random key makes every ciphertext equally likely for every plaintext.
State limitations: key as long as message, truly random key, one-time use and key distribution.
Mention key reuse attack through C1 ⊕ C2 = P1 ⊕ P2.

bank.q: Explain pseudorandom generators and stream ciphers. Use RC4 to describe how a keystream is produced and used.
outline: Define seed, expansion factor and pseudorandom output.
Define keystream S and encryption C_i = P_i ⊕ S_i.
Describe RC4 state, key scheduling and byte generation at a high level.
List required properties: no short period, no predictable bits and no key or nonce reuse.
State one weakness of RC4 related to biased initial output bytes.

bank.q: Describe the Feistel round. Prove informally why the same structure decrypts when the subkeys are used in reverse order.
outline: Split block into L and R halves.
Compute L′ = R and R′ = L ⊕ F(R, K_i).
Swap halves at the end of the round.
Show that applying the round with the same K_i recovers the previous halves.
Explain that F need not be invertible; only the subkey order changes in decryption.

bank.q: Describe DES encryption in detail: initial permutation, 16 Feistel rounds, key schedule, S-boxes and final permutation.
outline: State 64-bit block and 56-bit effective key.
Explain initial permutation and split into 32-bit halves.
Describe expansion, key mixing, S-box substitution and P-box permutation in each round.
Explain the 16 round subkeys produced by PC-1, shifts and PC-2.
State final swap and inverse initial permutation.
Mention why 56-bit key size is too small today.

bank.q: Explain the AES round transformations and key expansion for a 128-bit key.
outline: State 128-bit block and 10 rounds for 128-bit key, with 12 or 14 rounds for longer keys.
Describe SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns and AddRoundKey.
Explain that the last round omits MixColumns.
Describe key expansion using RotWord, SubWord, round constants and XOR.
Contrast AES byte operations with DES bit operations and Feistel half-swap.

bank.q: Compare ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR modes. Explain the role of the IV or counter and the effect of bit errors.
outline: Define a mode of operation and why it is needed.
Explain ECB pattern leakage and lack of chaining.
Explain CBC chaining with a random IV and error propagation.
Explain CFB and OFB as stream-like modes.
Explain CTR as counter encryption with parallel decryption and no padding.
State that IV or nonce must be unique and unpredictable where required.

bank.q: Define CPA and CCA security using attack games. Why does CCA security motivate message authentication codes?
outline: Describe the challenge ciphertext and indistinguishability game.
Define CPA: adversary may query encryption of chosen plaintexts.
Define CCA: adversary may also query decryption except on the challenge ciphertext.
Explain malleability of encryption without integrity.
Explain encrypt-then-MAC as a common CCA-secure construction.

bank.q: Given a toy Feistel round function F and a 8-bit block, compute one encryption round and then decrypt it by reversing the subkeys.
outline: Write L and R from the block.
Apply L′ = R and R′ = L ⊕ F(R, K).
Swap halves to form the round output.
Apply the same round with the same K in reverse order.
Show that the original block returns.

bank.q: A one-time pad key is reused for two messages. Show how an attacker recovers information from the two ciphertexts and state the fix.
outline: Write C1 = P1 ⊕ K and C2 = P2 ⊕ K.
Compute C1 ⊕ C2 = P1 ⊕ P2.
Explain how English text or known plaintext can recover P1 and P2.
State that the pad must be random, as long as the message, and never reused.

bank.q: Choose a block cipher mode for disk encryption, for a streaming link and for a small database field. Justify each choice with IV and error-propagation needs.
outline: For disk encryption, discuss CBC or XTS-like wide-block use and unique IV per sector.
For streaming, discuss CTR or CFB and nonce uniqueness.
For small fields, discuss ECB risks and why CBC with random IV may be preferred.
Mention padding, parallel access and integrity separately.

bank.q: For two-key triple DES, calculate the meet-in-the-middle attack cost roughly and compare it with single DES brute force.
outline: Write C = E_K3(D_K2(E_K1(P))) for three-key or two-key variant.
Explain meet-in-the-middle over two 56-bit keys.
State roughly 2^56 work and 2^56 storage for the two-key case.
Compare with 2^56 single DES brute force and 2^112 three-key naive search.
Conclude that two-key triple DES gives less than 112-bit security.

bank.q: Compare DES and AES designs: Feistel versus substitution-permutation network, block and key sizes, software speed, hardware cost and resistance to known attacks.
outline: Contrast Feistel half-swap with AES byte-oriented SPN.
Compare 64-bit and 128-bit blocks and 56-bit versus 128/192/256-bit keys.
Explain DES small key and 3DES slow repeated encryption.
Explain AES MixColumns and S-box diffusion.
Evaluate why AES replaced DES in practice.
Mention side-channel issues for both.

bank.q: Evaluate linear and differential cryptanalysis against modern block ciphers. How do CPA and CCA security definitions capture practical attacks better than simple key recovery?
outline: Define linear approximations and bias.
Define differential pairs and probability through rounds.
Explain how round count and S-box design reduce bias and differential probability.
State that AES was designed with resistance to these attacks.
Define CPA and CCA games and adversary advantage.
Explain why CCA security rules out malleability and motivates authenticated encryption.

glossary.def: A small change in plaintext or key should change about half the output bits.
The relation between key and ciphertext should be complex, usually through substitution.
Changes in one plaintext bit should spread over many ciphertext bits, usually through permutation or mixing.
A substitution table that maps a small input group to a small output group.
A permutation box that rearranges bits or bytes to spread influence.
The subkey mixed into one cipher round.
The algorithm that derives round keys from the master key.
A mode that encrypts each block independently, so equal plaintext blocks give equal ciphertext blocks.
A mode that XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encryption.
A mode that encrypts previous ciphertext to produce a keystream for the next plaintext segment.
A mode that repeatedly encrypts an IV to produce a keystream independent of plaintext.
A mode that encrypts successive counter values to form a keystream, allowing parallel operation.
A number used once to make encryptions under one key different.
A public starting value that randomizes a mode such as CBC or OFB.
An attack in which the adversary can obtain ciphertexts for plaintexts it chooses.
An attack in which the adversary can obtain decryptions for ciphertexts it chooses.
A keyed function that no efficient adversary can distinguish from a truly random function.
A keyed block cipher that no efficient adversary can distinguish from a truly random permutation.
A function that decreases faster than every inverse polynomial, used to bound adversary advantage.
Trying every possible key until the correct one is found.
A time-memory tradeoff attack on multiple encryption that searches two key parts from opposite ends.
A cipher design that alternates keyed substitution layers with permutation or mixing layers.
The finite field with 256 elements used by AES MixColumns arithmetic.
The fixed number of bits a block cipher encrypts in one operation.
